projects.title: Truck tracking
projects.summary: A redesign of shipment tracking inside FarMart OS, so business users can follow every delivery with clarity and confidence.
projects.overview: FarMart OS is the internal platform FarMart's operations teams use every day. Working with two product designers and the engineering team, I redesigned the truck tracking experience to make shipment visibility simpler and easier to trust.

projects.title: FarMart Dashak
projects.summary: Branding for FarMart's 10-year anniversary: one identity for a two-day celebration, from ten-year walls to trophies.
projects.deliverables: Event identity, walls, backdrops, flags, certificates, trophies, mementos, printables

sections.label: Overview
sections.big: FarMart Dashak was FarMart's tenth anniversary, a two-day, company-wide celebration. Day one was Sports Day; day two was the main anniversary function. Together with Akshay Sharma and Anjali Choudhary, I worked on the event's branding and visual design, taking one identity from ten-year walls and stage backdrops all the way down to certificates, trophies and mementos.

sections.label: Two days, two moods
items: Sports, team activities and employee participation, with its own sports awards.
The formal ten-year celebration: FarMart's journey, recognition and awards.

sections.label: The challenge
items: Work across both days of the event
Feel energetic for Sports Day and polished for the main function
Stay consistent across printed and physical materials
Scale from a large wall down to a certificate or trophy

sections.text: A complete branded experience, not a collection of event assets.

sections.label: Mapping the two days
body: I started by mapping what each day needed: the activities, the tone, and the awards. That showed where the identity had to stay fixed and where it could flex for the context.
I worked with FarMart's marketing and event teams throughout, from understanding requirements and exploring directions to incorporating feedback and preparing final files for production.

sections.label: One system, every size
sections.intro: The same visual language had to hold up across very different formats, each seen at a different distance:
items: Read in photos and from the audience
Glimpsed while moving through the space
sections.note: Large-format pieces had to work from a distance, while certificates, trophies and mementos needed finer, more refined detail. Everything was designed in Figma with physical production in mind.

sections.label: Key decisions
items: The milestone became the central visual element and the common thread connecting every asset and both days.
Instead of separate branding for each day, a shared system that adapts, so the days feel connected while keeping their own character.
Take the identity off the wall
The branding extended into certificates, trophies and mementos, so the identity became something employees could take home.
A long white wall titled 'Every chapter led us here. The story continues.' A timeline runs from 2016 to 2026 with milestones and a band of photos from FarMart's decade.
The 10-year wall: FarMart's decade as a timeline, from 2016 to 2026.
A white entrance arch with the 10 FarMart dashak lockup, leading down a green carpet lined with feather flags.
The entrance arch and flags leading into the venue.
A large standee reading '10 years of innovation and impact', with 3D letters for the illustrated 10 and the dashak wordmark.
Signage at the venue: the illustrated 10 as a 3D object.
A dark backdrop with the illustrated green 10, the FarMart logo and the dashak wordmark in white.
The dark version of the lockup on the event backdrop.

sections.label: Outcome
sections.intro: The branding ran across both days of the celebration, with one visual language across:

sections.label: Team
sections.outro: Working with FarMart's marketing and event teams.

sections.label: What I learned
sections.big: Designing beyond the screen. Physical production meant thinking about viewing distance, scale and the object in someone's hand, not just a frame in Figma.

projects.title: Waffle
projects.summary: A browser cooking game you play with your hands and voice. Take an order, make the batter, mix, cook and top your waffle, then get scored out of three stars. Designed and built solo in about a week.
projects.deliverables: Game concept, visual direction, illustrations, UI, live web game

sections.label: Overview
sections.big: Waffle is a browser game about making a waffle, played with your hands and your voice. Hand tracking with MediaPipe and voice recognition replace the mouse and keyboard, so an everyday cooking routine becomes something you perform. It's a personal project: I designed and built it on my own, from idea to a live, playable game, in about a week.

sections.label: The idea
body: It started with reels of MediaPipe and TouchDesigner experiments: people controlling visuals just by moving their hands. I wanted to see how that kind of interaction would feel inside a simple, familiar game, so I picked something everyone already knows how to do: making a waffle.

items: The Waffle kitchen: an illustrated counter with sugar, eggs, baking powder, vanilla, butter, flour and milk around a mixing bowl. A checklist on the left tracks Waffle Batter 0 of 7; panels on the right show camera tracking, a pinch gesture guide and voice control.
Stage one: pick seven ingredients for the batter, by pinching or by voice.

sections.label: A round, step by step
items: A customer orders a waffle, like a Strawberry Supreme for Ishaan, with the toppings it needs.
Point at each of the seven ingredients and pinch to pick it up, then open your palm to drop it in the bowl. Or just say “add milk”.
Circle your index finger in the air to stir, drag circles inside the bowl, or say “mix”. A progress bar fills as you go.
A timer runs while the waffle cooks. When it turns golden brown, a ding tells you it's ready.
Pinch the right toppings from a tray of seven, or say a topping, then “serve”.
Up to three stars, with your time, your best score, and a button to share your waffle.

sections.label: Three ways to play
head: Stage
Hands
Voice
Mouse
rows: Point and pinch to pick, open palm to add
No input: wait for the ding
Point at a topping and pinch
sections.note: Each stage names its gesture and its voice command on screen, and the cooking stage uses sound instead: a ding at golden brown, so you don't have to stare at the timer.

items: A top-down bowl of flour, egg, butter, sugar and vanilla with a whisk. A banner reads Mix the Batter, 0 percent: circle your index finger, or drag circles inside the bowl.
Stage two: stir by circling a finger in the air.

A plain waffle on a plate. An order card for Ishaan lists Strawberry Supreme: strawberry, whipped cream and chocolate. A tray below offers seven toppings. The camera panel warns: hand not visible, move your hand into view.
Toppings, with live camera feedback when your hand leaves the frame.

sections.text: Anyone should be able to start playing without instructions.

sections.label: The challenge
body: Gesture and voice controls are unfamiliar for most people. The hard part was making the cooking process understandable through visual interaction alone, while keeping it simple enough for a casual player with no gaming experience.

So the game coaches you the whole time. A gesture guide shows the move for the current stage, the camera panel reports what it sees (“Hand not visible”, “Move your hand into view”), a checklist tracks every ingredient and topping, a warning appears the moment tracking is lost, and a ding tells you when the waffle is done.

sections.label: Key decisions
items: So players understand what to do in seconds, even with unfamiliar controls.
The batter, the cooking waffle and the finished waffle each look different, and checklists and progress bars show how far along you are.
A persistent gesture guide, live camera status and a voice prompt for every stage, with a mouse fallback where it helps.
Every object was designed to belong to the same warm kitchen, so the game feels like one experience rather than a collection of separate assets.

A result card reading Practice round, Chef's kiss, with three gold stars and a photo of a strawberry, cream and chocolate waffle. Cooked to a perfect golden brown; every topping was right. Time 3:05. Buttons: Share my waffle and Next order.
The payoff: three stars, a time to beat, and a waffle to share.
Waffle open on a MacBook at a desk, mid-way through picking butter for the batter.
Waffle in the wild, picking butter for the batter.

sections.label: One visual system
sections.intro: A warm, playful cooking-game style, with illustrated objects and clear visual states that work together:

sections.label: Built with AI
sections.unit: from idea to a live game
sections.note: I built Waffle with Claude and ChatGPT, which let me move from concept to visual design to working computer vision and voice controls, and ship a playable game in about a week.

sections.label: What's next
body: More toppings are next. I also haven't playtested it formally yet, so watching people play for the first time is the other step I want to take.

projects.title: Kirana Club
projects.summary: Content and campaign creatives for India's kirana store owners: busy people who give a banner or video only a glance.
projects.deliverables: Short-form video, thumbnails, in-app banners, brand creatives
projects.overview: At Kirana Club I produced and edited daily video content for the app and social platforms, designed in-app banners and promotional creatives, and worked with consumer brands on bespoke campaign creatives.
projects.outcome: Average daily viewership grew to around 6,000 to 6,500 views, and the data-informed banners significantly improved click-through rates on key campaigns.

sections.label: Overview
sections.big: Kirana Club is a community app for kirana and small retail shop owners, mostly in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities. They use it to discover products, check mandi rates, manage orders and find offers and schemes. I joined the content and marketing team as a visual designer, making the app's videos, banners and brand campaigns easier to notice and faster to understand.

sections.label: Who I designed for
body: A kirana owner opens the app between customers. They're busy, often more comfortable reading Hindi, and they don't owe any creative their attention. Generic social-media styling, with decorative layouts and clever copy, wasn't built for them.
So everything I made had to pass one test, in a glance:

sections.text: Why should I stop and look at this?

sections.label: What the team needed
items: More views and engagement on video content
Content that was easier to discover in the app
Offers and products explained clearly, fast
Brand-partner creatives that still felt like the partner's brand

sections.label: One rule for every creative
sections.intro: The most important information had to be the most visually dominant. For promotional creatives I worked to a fixed order:
tiers: What's in it for the shop owner
A real product photo, not a generic graphic
sections.note: For this audience, bold type, strong product imagery and simple Hindi were usually more effective than complex or decorative layouts.

sections.label: The rule, in practice
sections.alt: An Aashirvaad Soya Chunks banner in Hindi. Left: 'Tasty soya, great profit' and a red box reading 'Only ₹7.35!', with 'best rate' below. Right: two soya chunk packs with a yellow '36% margin' badge. Bottom bar: 'Stock up on ITC Aashirvaad soya' and an 'Order' button.
marks: Offer: only ₹7.35, and a 36% margin badge
sections.caption: Aashirvaad Soya Chunks. The price and the margin do the talking; the order button waits at the end.

sections.label: A daily content engine
body: I supported roughly one video or content piece a day. That pace only works with a system, so instead of designing every video from scratch I built reusable patterns for typography, headlines, product placement, backgrounds, brand elements and information hierarchy.
It made production faster and kept every piece recognisably Kirana Club, whether it was a retail tip, an offer, mandi and market updates, a trending topic or a brand message.

sections.label: What I changed in the videos
items: Stronger hooks in the opening moments
Shorter messages that are easy to take in
Hindi and simple language where it helped
Thumbnails designed to be noticed in a busy feed

sections.label: In-app banners
body: Banners carried offers and schemes, new products, campaigns and brand messages. For April's scheme offers, like GoDesi's bumper scheme and the Zoff Haldi Loot offer, three order tiers had to be comparable in a single glance. I also designed formats for the Punji reward scheme and for product and category communication.
Where past performance data was available, it shaped what to emphasise: the offer or the price, product photos or generic graphics, Hindi or English, and how visible the call to action should be.

items: A Johnson's Baby banner: 'Get a flat 28% margin' next to a baby powder bottle, and a bar below: MRP ₹125 per pack, retailer margin 28%, 'Your earnings: ₹35 per pack'.
Johnson's Baby: the offer translated into what the shop owner earns per pack.
A yellow Sunfeast banner with a giant melting chocolate number 5: '5 Bourbon biscuits, now just ₹5!', next to a Bourbon pack and biscuits.
Sunfeast Bourbon: the price becomes the picture.
A Mangaldeep dhoop banner: '12+2' crossed out above a bold '12+4 FREE', a '10% extra profit' badge, four fragrance packs, and a row of other flavours.
Mangaldeep: the upgrade from 12+2 to 12+4 is read in one glance.
An Anmol banner: a hand bursts through paper holding a 2 in 1 biscuit pack. Text: 'Fast-selling Anmol biscuit. Stock up, grow profit!', available at ₹5, ₹10 and ₹20.
Anmol 2 in 1: playful, but it still ends in 'stock up, grow profit'.
A Sugandh tea banner: 'Up to 30% assured margin' and three product cards for masala, elaichi and Climax tea, each with MRP, price and margin, over a black 'Order' bar.
A Cravitos Raksha Bandhan banner: 'Boost sales this Raksha Bandhan' and three sweet boxes on cards with margin tags, MRP and price, over a black 'Order' bar.
sections.caption: One template, two brands: Sugandh Chai and Cravitos share the same card layout for product, MRP, price and margin, and the same order bar.

sections.label: Tiered schemes
items: A tall GoDesi banner: 'Offer valid till 18 April', 'Bumper scheme on GoDesi', then three rows: orders of ₹800+, ₹1500+ and ₹2500+ earn 10, 30 and 60 imli pops free. The ₹1500 row has a green border. A green 'Order now' button at the bottom.

A tall orange 'Haldi Loot Offer' banner shaped like tickets: orders of ₹1500+, ₹2800+ and ₹4000+ earn 10, 20 and 30 packets of turmeric free, then 'Free turmeric, 7.5% more profit' with Zoff turmeric packs, and a yellow 'Order now' button.
notes: Thresholds on the left, rewards on the right, in matching rows, so tiers compare in one glance.
GoDesi's middle tier gets a green border, nudging shop owners toward the ₹1500 order.
The deadline sits at the top as a small chip, the single order button at the bottom.
Haldi Loot closes on the profit: 7.5% more, next to the product.
sections.caption: April schemes for GoDesi and Zoff, designed for the phone screen.

sections.label: In the app
sections.intro: This is where the work lived: inside a busy feed, next to mandi rates, schemes and retailer posts. On a screen this crowded, a creative only works if its message lands before the thumb scrolls on.
items: The Johnson's Baby brand page in the Kirana Club app, with a post announcing new small packs at ₹25 and ₹30.
Johnson's Baby's brand page, with the new small-pack offer.

A Kwality Wall's post in the feed: 'Guaranteed extra profit with Kwality Wall's. Take a freezer, get 20%+ extra profit.' It shows 437 likes, 348 comments and 19 WhatsApp shares. The retailer's name in the comment is blurred.
A Kwality Wall's post: 437 likes, 348 comments, 19 shares.

A Mandi Report video post titled Kirana Samachar: a presenter, a photo of groundnut oil, a price table for edible oils and a headline ticker. It shows 816 likes and 1,000 comments. Faces and names are blurred.
The Mandi Report video format: 816 likes, 1,000 comments.

sections.label: Brand partnerships
sections.intro: I made campaign, product and promotional creatives for FMCG and consumer brands, including:

items: A purple Mangaldeep campaign banner for the Sigma Dhamaka gift scheme, 1 July to 31 October 2025, with a marquee badge and prizes including a motorbike, a phone and trips to Singapore and Dubai.
Sigma Dhamaka: a campaign identity for Mangaldeep's gift scheme, not just a single offer.

sections.note: Brands supplied their product shots and campaign photography; I designed the layouts, typography and hierarchy around them. The balance in every project was the partner's own brand identity against Kirana Club's audience and communication style.

sections.label: Outcome
sections.note: Daily viewership grew clearly over my time on the content, reaching roughly 6,000 to 6,500 views a day. Individual posts drew real conversation too: 437 likes and 348 comments on one Kwality Wall's post, and 816 likes and 1,000 comments on a Mandi Report video. The offer and the brand matter as much as the design, but the creatives had to earn the stop first.

sections.label: What I learned
sections.big: Designing for one specific audience changes everything. Kirana owners have little time and different needs from a typical consumer app's users, so clarity, relevance, language and hierarchy mattered far more than style. I carry that into every product I design now.
